frase_gancho.texto: The largest court in the city, with a macaw that now lives in another museum.

puente_narrativo.texto: Continue your route: just a few steps away is another space that tells how time was measured in the city.

guion_corto.texto: Shaped like a capital letter I, this is the largest ballcourt in Xochicalco. It sits on the lowest terrace and still preserves two of its markers. A sculpture in the shape of a macaw was found here, and today it is on display in the National Museum of Anthropology. Medina Romero, the site director, explains that Xochicalco had three courts and that this one, the largest and the easiest to reach, may have served the general population. The ball game was a sport, but also a ritual. It was played with a rubber ball, and the court, with its sloping walls, was a space of rules, wagers, and ceremony.

guion_largo.texto:
There are places that you recognize by their shape. This one has the shape of a capital letter I.

The INAH guide explains that the south ballcourt is on the fifth terrace, the lowest, and that it preserves two markers in place. The markers were stones set into the walls of the court. In this court, a macaw sculpture was also found. Today it is in the National Museum of Anthropology.

Medina Romero, the site director, notes that Xochicalco had three courts oriented toward three of the four cardinal directions. The southern one is the largest and the easiest to reach, and for that reason it is thought to have served the general population. Hirth counts five: three on the main hill and two more on neighboring hills.

The ball game was played with a solid rubber ball. According to the site descriptions, the players struck it with their hips. The sloping walls of the court helped the ball rebound and stay in play.

The ball game was much more than a sport. In Mesoamerica it had a ritual side and a political side. The matches could be ceremonies, and the courts, gathering places for the community.

If you are standing on the court, notice its shape. Imagine two teams, a heavy ball going back and forth, and spectators along the sides. The sound of rubber against stone, the shouts, the dust.

It was not a hidden building. It was a court for everyone.

texto.pregunta: Myth: The ball game was just a sport.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It was a game, but also a ritual and a political space for the community.
